reviews.author: Lorenzo (ARM)
reviews.summary: Reviewer noted that the patch does not explicitly check for shadow stacks in hmm_vma_walk_test() and requested a check be added to prevent devices from gaining write access to shadow stacks.
reviews.raw_body:
On Fri, Nov 13, 2026 at 02:55:36PM -0500, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> HMM can grant ordinary device write access to a userspace shadow stack.
> On x86, pte_write() is true for a shadow-stack PTE, so a populated page
> can be returned with HMM_PFN_WRITE without taking a CPU write fault.
>
> Nouveau translates that flag into a writable GPU mapping.
>
> Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(). Use the existing
> unsupported-range handling: a requested fault returns -EFAULT, while a
> snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
>
> Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20261111-mason-migrate-et-al-fixes-v1-10-3d2454362e8d@kernel.org/
> Fixes: 54007f818206 ("mm: Introduce VM_SHADOW_STACK for shadow stack memory")
> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
> Cc: "Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM)" <ljs@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>

Thanks for doing the HMM side of this, LGTM and:

Reviewed-by: Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM) <ljs@kernel.org>

> ---
>  mm/hmm.c | 3 +++
>  1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)
>
> diff --git a/mm/hmm.c b/mm/hmm.c
> index 2f1e98c6b644..fa61ca59d927 100644
> --- a/mm/hmm.c
> +++ b/mm/hmm.c
> @@ -596,6 +596,7 @@ static int hmm_vma_walk_test(unsigned long start, unsigned long end,
>  	struct vm_area_struct *vma = walk->vma;
>
>  	if (!(vma->vm_flags & (VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP)) &&
> +	    !vma_test_single_mask(vma, VMA_SHADOW_STACK) &&
>  	    vma->vm_flags & VM_READ)
>  		return 0;
>
> @@ -607,6 +608,8 @@ static int hmm_vma_walk_test(unsigned long start, unsigned long end,
>  	 * allow write access either. HMM does not support architectures that
>  	 * allow write without read.
>  	 *
> +	 * Devices must not gain ordinary write access to shadow stacks.
> +	 *
>  	 * If a fault is requested for an unsupported range then it is a hard
>  	 * failure.
>  	 */
> --
> 2.56.0
>

--
Cheers, Lorenzo

On 11/14/26 08:25, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> On 2026-11-13 20:20 -0400, Jason Gunthorpe wrote:
>> On Fri, Nov 13, 2026 at 03:41:33PM -0500, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
>>>
>>> Some of the context is here:
>>> https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261111-mason-migrate-et-al-fixes-v1-10-3d2454362e8d@kernel.org/
>>>
>>> We had a similar issue with migration, but this should handle the DMA
>>> case as well.
>>>
>>> It's "technically writable" but the kernel is supposed to prevent that.
>>
>> Bah, it's not writable at all. The CPU PTE has write disabled and
>> someone thought it was a good idea to make pte_write() return true
>> because the CPU allows writes through a special instruction on this
>> special PTE? So now all the places like this think its writable, when
>> it really isn't.
>>
> 
> I completely missed this, that will teach me to trust pte_write() I
> guess... what a bizarre design choice.  I'm sure there's "reasons".
> 
>> You could also fix this by having something like pte_real_write() or
>> whatever that doesn't lie about the write bit in the PTE :|
>>
> 
> or rename pte_write() to pte_fake_write() instead and restore
> pte_write() to its former truthful glory

It's writable by the hardware, that's what matters to core-mm, for example, when
it comes to things like fork(), mproetect() etc.

*nobody* besides selected core-mm code should ever write to random PTEs. They
shouldn't ever even care about pte_write().

We have GUP for that, which takes care of that oddity properly when deciding
whether we can *actually* write to a mapped page.

Well, and we have HMM that reimplements part of GUP in ugly ways (sorry) that we
missed.

-- 
Cheers,

David

---

On 11/19/26 21:05, Dave Hansen wrote:
> On 11/14/26 17:01, Andrew Morton wrote:
>> On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
>> rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
>> shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
>> HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
>> RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
>> registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
>> to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
>> potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
>>
>> Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
>> A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
> 
> This is a fun one.
> 
> I almost wonder if we want to go one step further and disallow GUPs with
> FOLL_WRITE on these PTEs. There should be precious few reasons for
> devices to be writing to shadow stack pages.
> 
> Isn't this a bigger issue than HMM? Should the fix be in HMM?

I think we discussed this excessively after I raised it and it's even partially
documented in the relevant commit messages.

-- 
Cheers,

David

---

On 11/19/26 21:40, Edgecombe, Rick P wrote:
> On Thu, 2026-11-19 at 12:05 -0800, Dave Hansen wrote:
>> On 11/14/26 17:01, Andrew Morton wrote:
>>> On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear. The CPU
>>> rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
>>> shadow-stack instructions can write it. HMM consequently sets
>>> HMM_PFN_WRITE. Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
>>> RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
>>> registered memory region. A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
>>> to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
>>> potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
>>>
>>> Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
>>> A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
>>
>> This is a fun one.
>>
>> I almost wonder if we want to go one step further and disallow GUPs with
>> FOLL_WRITE on these PTEs. There should be precious few reasons for
>> devices to be writing to shadow stack pages.
>>
>> Isn't this a bigger issue than HMM? Should the fix be in HMM?
> 
> We do reject GUPs to shadow stack PTEs with FOLL_WRITE, unless FOLL_FORCE is
> passed. The tricky thing as mentioned my others in this thread is that shadow
> stack memory *is* writable by userspace. But also the kernel should not treat it
> as such
> 
> A false negative for pte_write() is dangerous when the kernel needs to decide
> when to revoke access. (i.e. fork) I think a mistake there is somewhat worse
> then missing an exotic way to cajole the kernel into writing to a user's shadow
> stack like this. So I think pte_write() being true for shadow stacks is the
> correct implementation.
> 
> But, maybe the problem is that pte_write() is doing the job of two separate
> concepts. What if there was a pte_userspace_could_write() and a
> pte_kernel_should_not_write()? Names would need some work...

Gah, nak,

pte_write() just says "something might be able to write to it".

If that's actually true depends on other factors. Like the access+dirty on HW
that manages that in software.

I repeat: *no code* in Linux besides core-mm should ever interpret "pte_write()"
as "cool, I can write to it". The exception is GUP and unfortunately HMM.

-- 
Cheers,

David

reviews.author: Jason Gunthorpe
reviews.summary: Reviewer Jason Gunthorpe noted that the shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear on x86, but pte_write() reports it writable because shadow-stack instructions can write to it; this allows HMM to set HMM_PFN_WRITE, which Nouveau and RDMA use for GPU and device write permission respectively, potentially allowing a device or RDMA peer to overwrite the process's shadow stack. He suggested adding details about this behavior in the patch description.
reviews.raw_body:
On Fri, Nov 13, 2026 at 02:55:36PM -0500, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> HMM can grant ordinary device write access to a userspace shadow stack.
> On x86, pte_write() is true for a shadow-stack PTE, so a populated page
> can be returned with HMM_PFN_WRITE without taking a CPU write fault.

I'm not sure I understand this? The pte is writable but you don't want
only DMA to write to it?

Is there something special on x86 that makes the shadow stack pte
non-writable by the CPU?

A few more words here would help

Regardless, this seems reasonable to me, there is no use case to
write to the shadow stack..

Reviewed-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@nvidia.com>

Jason

---

> > > can be returned with HMM_PFN_WRITE without taking a CPU write fault.
> > 
> > I'm not sure I understand this? The pte is writable but you don't want
> > only DMA to write to it?
> >
> > Is there something special on x86 that makes the shadow stack pte
> > non-writable by the CPU?
> >
> 
> Some of the context is here:
> https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261111-mason-migrate-et-al-fixes-v1-10-3d2454362e8d@kernel.org/
> 
> We had a similar issue with migration, but this should handle the DMA
> case as well.
> 
> It's "technically writable" but the kernel is supposed to prevent that.

Bah, it's not writable at all. The CPU PTE has write disabled and
someone thought it was a good idea to make pte_write() return true
because the CPU allows writes through a special instruction on this
special PTE? So now all the places like this think its writable, when
it really isn't.

You could also fix this by having something like pte_real_write() or
whatever that doesn't lie about the write bit in the PTE :|

The patch is still fine, in that it matches what everything else does,
but I'd include these details someplace..

Jason

---

> How does this look for an altered changelog?

that is far more common..

Thanks,
Jason

> > : Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.  A
> > : requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
> 
> Yes, but it is not just nouveau, RDMA user can do this too and
> that is far more common..

Thanks.  This?

On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.

Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.

reviews.author: David (Arm)
reviews.summary: reviewer noted that pte_write() is sufficient for core-mm's needs, and that nobody besides selected core-mm code should write to random PTEs; they suggested using GUP instead of reimplementing it in HMM
reviews.raw_body:
It's writable by the hardware, that's what matters to core-mm, for example, when
it comes to things like fork(), mproetect() etc.

*nobody* besides selected core-mm code should ever write to random PTEs. They
shouldn't ever even care about pte_write().

We have GUP for that, which takes care of that oddity properly when deciding
whether we can *actually* write to a mapped page.

Well, and we have HMM that reimplements part of GUP in ugly ways (sorry) that we
missed.

-- 
Cheers,

David

reviews.author: Dave Hansen
reviews.summary: Reviewer Dave Hansen noted that on x86, shadow-stack PTEs have their ordinary write bit clear, but pte_write() reports them writable due to shadow-stack instructions; this allows devices or RDMA peers to overwrite the process's shadow stack, potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing protection. He suggested rejecting shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access, and also considered disallowing GUPs with FOLL_WRITE on these PTEs.
reviews.raw_body:
On 11/14/26 17:01, Andrew Morton wrote:
> On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
> rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
> shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
> HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
> RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
> registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
> to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
> potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
> 
> Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
> A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.

This is a fun one.

I almost wonder if we want to go one step further and disallow GUPs with
FOLL_WRITE on these PTEs. There should be precious few reasons for
devices to be writing to shadow stack pages.

Isn't this a bigger issue than HMM? Should the fix be in HMM?

reviews.author: Edgecombe, P
reviews.summary: Reviewer noted that shadow-stack PTEs have their ordinary write bit clear, but pte_write() reports them writable because shadow-stack instructions can write to them; this allows devices or RDMA peers with write access to overwrite the process's shadow stack, potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing protection. The reviewer suggested rejecting shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access, and proposed considering a separate pte_userspace_could_write() function to handle user-space writable PTEs.
reviews.raw_body:
On Sat, 2026-11-14 at 17:01 -0800, Andrew Morton wrote:
> Thanks.  This?
> 
> On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
> rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
> shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
> HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
> RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
> registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
> to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
> potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
> 
> Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
> A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.

BTW, this is not just an x86 thing. Arm and riscv have the same pte_write()
shadow stack behavior for the same reasons. Despite not having the
Write=0,Dirty=1 thing, which *is* weird. But they still try to prevent the
kernel from writing it via logic in gup, etc.

---

On Thu, 2026-11-19 at 12:05 -0800, Dave Hansen wrote:
> On 11/14/26 17:01, Andrew Morton wrote:
> > On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
> > rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
> > shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
> > HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
> > RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
> > registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
> > to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
> > potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
> > 
> > Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
> > A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
> 
> This is a fun one.
> 
> I almost wonder if we want to go one step further and disallow GUPs with
> FOLL_WRITE on these PTEs. There should be precious few reasons for
> devices to be writing to shadow stack pages.
> 
> Isn't this a bigger issue than HMM? Should the fix be in HMM?

We do reject GUPs to shadow stack PTEs with FOLL_WRITE, unless FOLL_FORCE is
passed. The tricky thing as mentioned my others in this thread is that shadow
stack memory *is* writable by userspace. But also the kernel should not treat it
as such

A false negative for pte_write() is dangerous when the kernel needs to decide
when to revoke access. (i.e. fork) I think a mistake there is somewhat worse
then missing an exotic way to cajole the kernel into writing to a user's shadow
stack like this. So I think pte_write() being true for shadow stacks is the
correct implementation.

But, maybe the problem is that pte_write() is doing the job of two separate
concepts. What if there was a pte_userspace_could_write() and a
pte_kernel_should_not_write()? Names would need some work...
